topic: Bayes' Theorem: The Geometry of Changing Your Mind
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students with a basic grasp of probability

outline.topic: Bayes' Theorem: The Geometry of Changing Your Mind
outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students with a basic grasp of probability

sections.title: The Core Intuition: Probability as Space
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite concept: Probability is not just a number, but an 'area' within a total space of possibilities. We represent the entire world of possibilities as a 1x1 square (Area = 1).
sections.example: Imagine a 10x10 grid representing a forest. If 10% of the forest contains Rare Blue butterflies, we color 10% of the square's area blue. This is our 'Prior' belief before seeing any evidence.

sections.title: The Scenario: Prior Probabilities
sections.content: Establish a base rate (Prior) using a character-driven example. Split the square vertically into two rectangles based on the initial probability of two competing hypotheses.
sections.example: A robot detective is looking for a 'Glitch-Bot'. In a factory, 20% are Glitch-Bots (Small Rectangle) and 80% are Normal-Bots (Large Rectangle). Visually, the square is now split 2:8.

sections.title: The Evidence: Conditional Likelihood
sections.content: Introduce new evidence that has different 'hit rates' for each hypothesis. Graphically, we slice the horizontal axis of our existing rectangles. This creates sub-areas representing 'True Positives' and 'False Positives'.
sections.example: The detective uses a 'Spark Test'. 90% of Glitch-Bots spark, but 10% of Normal-Bots also spark by accident. We shade the top 90% of the Glitch-Bot rectangle and the top 10% of the Normal-Bot rectangle.

sections.title: The Geometric Update: Slicing the Universe
sections.content: When evidence occurs (the 'Spark' happens), the 'non-sparking' areas of our square vanish. They are no longer possible. Our 'universe' of possibilities shrinks to only the shaded areas.
sections.example: The robot sparks! We visually discard the bottom (non-sparking) parts of the square. We are left with a thin slice from the Normal-Bots and a tall slice from the Glitch-Bots.

sections.title: The Posterior: Re-normalizing the World
sections.content: The final step of Bayes' Theorem: Re-stretching the remaining area to fill a 1x1 square again. The 'Posterior' probability is the ratio of the 'True Evidence' area to the 'Total Evidence' area.
sections.example: We compare the area of (Glitch-Bots who spark) against the total area of (All bots who spark). Even though the test is 90% accurate, because Normal-Bots were so common, the resulting 'New Area' for Glitch-Bots might only be 69%.

sections.title: From Geometry to Formula
sections.content: Translate the visual stretching and slicing into the algebraic form of Bayes' Theorem, showing how each term corresponds to a geometric transformation.
sections.example: P(H|E) = [P(E|H) * P(H)] / P(E). We show that the numerator is the 'True Positive' area and the denominator is the 'Total Shaded' area.

storyboard.title: The Core Intuition: Probability as Space
lecture_lines: Imagine all possibilities fit inside a unit square.
The total area of this square equals one.
We represent probability as a specific area within it.
animations: Draw a square outline (color: #FFFFFF) representing the universe of possibilities.
Fill the interior of the square with a dark grey (#333333).
Fade in the text 'Area = 1' at the center of the square.
Transform a portion of the square to blue (#3498DB), covering 10% of the total area.
Draw a line and label 'Event: 10% Probability' pointing to the blue area.

storyboard.title: The Scenario: Prior Probabilities
lecture_lines: Meet a robot detective hunting for a Glitch-Bot.
Only twenty percent of bots in this factory glitch.
We split our square to show this prior belief.
animations: Divide the square vertically into two regions: 20% width (red: #E74C3C) and 80% width (green: #2ECC71).
Label the red region 'Glitch-Bot' and the green region 'Normal-Bot'.
Pulse the 'Glitch-Bot' label to emphasize the initial belief (Prior).

storyboard.title: The Evidence: Conditional Likelihood
lecture_lines: The detective uses a Spark Test on a bot.
Ninety percent of Glitch-Bots spark when tested.
But ten percent of Normal-Bots also spark.
We slice the rectangles to show these likelihoods.
Shaded areas represent the chance of seeing a spark.
animations: Shade the top 90% of the red region with a brighter red (#FF5555) to represent 'Sparks'.
Shade the top 10% of the green region with a brighter green (#55FF55) to represent 'Sparks'.
Label the bright red area 'True Positive' and the bright green area 'False Positive'.
Dim the lower 10% of the red region and lower 90% of the green region to near-black (#111111).
Highlight the horizontal 'slicing' line that separates sparking from non-sparking.

storyboard.title: The Geometric Update: Slicing the Universe
lecture_lines: Suddenly, the robot detective sees a bright spark.
Non-sparking possibilities are now impossible in our world.
We discard the bottom sections of our probability square.
Our universe shrinks to only the shaded regions.
Only two possible paths to a spark remain.
animations: Animate the near-black 'non-sparking' regions fading out to total black (#000000).
Shift the remaining 'True Positive' and 'False Positive' blocks together to the left.
Draw a brace under both blocks and label it 'Total Evidence: P(E)'.

storyboard.title: The Posterior: Re-normalizing the World
lecture_lines: We must find the new probability of a Glitch-Bot.
Compare the Glitch-Spark area to the total spark area.
We stretch these remaining areas to fill the square.
This re-normalization reveals our updated posterior belief.
The Glitch-Bot probability is now roughly sixty-nine percent.
animations: Scale the height of the two blocks until they reach the top of the frame.
Scale the widths of both blocks proportionally so their total width equals the original square's width.
Change the color of the 'Glitch-Bot' slice to a bright gold (#F1C40F).
Display the calculated posterior percentage '69.2%' inside the gold region.
Highlight the boundary between the two regions to show the final probability split.

storyboard.title: From Geometry to Formula
lecture_lines: This geometric process is exactly what Bayes' Theorem describes.
The numerator represents the specific shaded Glitch-Spark area.
Dividing by the total shaded area gives the posterior.
animations: Display the equation P(H|E) = [P(E|H) * P(H)] / P(E) in white (#FFFFFF).
Draw a box around the numerator and point it to the 'True Positive' area from the previous step.
Draw a box around the denominator and point it to the 'Total Evidence' area.
